sm: Hosts Myrna Brown and Mary Reichard open the November nineteenth edition of The World and Everything In It, previewing stories on child safety on Roblox, a three-way nuclear summit, and a campus incident. Kent Covington gives the news. President Trump was greeted by Xi Jinping with a red carpet ceremony in Shenzhen, China, ahead of a meeting with Xi and Vladimir Putin on Ukraine, Iran, and a possible nuclear agreement. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth announced a new military training deal with Venezuela and then flew to Colombia. House Democrats voted two hundred fifty-one to eleven to nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker. Mary Peltola won Alaska's Senate race, giving Democrats a fifty-six to forty-four majority, and an appeals court let twenty-seven transgender troops remain in uniform for now.

Mary Reichard interviews Andrea Stricker of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies about the summit in Shenzhen, held alongside the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting. Stricker says having two near peer nuclear rivals complicates American planning and could push the US toward more warheads. She is not optimistic about a breakthrough and expects at most declaratory statements about avoiding nuclear war and possible follow-on talks. She says verification would rely on satellites and intelligence rather than inspections, and that China, Russia, and Iran have prepositioned cyber threats. The show then turns to Roblox, where Marine veteran Woody Doe told senators that at age eleven he was pressured into sending photos by a user who claimed to be a student.

Woody Doe testified that when he went to meet the user, an older man answered the door and assaulted him, and that he stayed silent for years. About one hundred forty million people use Roblox daily, and three in four American children ages nine to twelve are signed up. Senator Josh Hawley asked whether children are safe, and witness Michael Schlepp, who created decoy accounts, said it was unbelievably easy for predators to reach children. A legal expert noted that turning off chat does not disable chats built by outside developers. Professor Miriam Gillis said Roblox's terms limit fines and push cases into private arbitration. Senators Hawley and Dick Durbin introduced a bill letting exploited children sue, and a similar bill might pass with the defense authorization act.

The next story concerns Kimmy, a graduate student at the University of Maryland Eastern Shore who served as a student host at a homecoming gospel concert. A performer known as B Slade, who identifies as an LGBTQ gospel singer, took the stage, and Kimmy said she and her team prayed and fasted beforehand. She then read a Bible passage from First Corinthians and said that anyone who supports what they witnessed goes against the word. Her microphone was cut, some of the crowd jeered, and others applauded. The university apologized to performers and audience members, not to her. Kimmy, who became a Christian at nineteen, says she takes nothing back. A brief item notes that James Blunt filed to change his name to Ryan Air after his album reached number one. A segment on aging begins.

The aging segment features Manel Weiss, whose group of friends agreed not to pursue plastic surgery, and theologians Kelly Kapic and Jen Wilkin. Kapic says finitude, or being a creature with limits, is called good. Wilkin, author of Dust to Dust, says an aging body can bear witness to the work of time and make others regard time as more precious. She says deep relationships help us see beauty, recalling her father, who still tells her she is beautiful, and she urges churches to value older members and ask what we are becoming. Commentator Daniel Sir then urges calm about artificial intelligence after recent tech failures, noting no evidence that AI caused them, and calls for protecting kids, countering hostile actors, and keeping markets free.
